title: Band-minimum degeneracy is not enough: density-of-states control of low-density ferromagnetism
abstract: Recent ultracold-atom experiments have observed ferromagnetic correlations in a geometrically tunable Fermi--Hubbard lattice at intermediate densities. Motivated by subsequent theoretical work that connected the low-density limit of the same model to the Mueller--Hartmann mechanism for itinerant ferromagnetism, we investigate the stability of ferromagnetism across a broad density range using the T-matrix approximation, a controlled approach in the dilute limit. We reproduce the ferromagnetic regime observed experimentally at intermediate densities and systematically compare finite-size and thermodynamic-limit calculations in the dilute regime. We find that the low-density ferromagnetic phase reported for the one-diagonal hopping lattice is strongly suppressed with increasing system size and disappears in the thermodynamic limit, indicating that it originates from finite-size effects. By contrast, low-density ferromagnetism remains robust in the square-lattice Hubbard model with hopping along both diagonal directions. We show that this qualitative difference cannot be explained by the degeneracy of the band minima alone, which occurs in both models. Instead, it is controlled by the singular behavior of the density of states at the band bottom: a weak divergence is insufficient to stabilize ferromagnetism, whereas a much stronger quasi-one-dimensional singularity supports a fully polarized ground state even in the dilute limit. Our results demonstrate that band-minimum degeneracy alone is not sufficient for low-density ferromagnetism and that the nature of the band-bottom density-of-states singularity ultimately controls its stability.
summary: This work investigates the conditions required for low-density ferromagnetism in Fermi-Hubbard models realized with ultracold atoms. By comparing two lattice geometries, the authors demonstrate that while both exhibit band degeneracy, only the model with a stronger quasi-one-dimensional density of states singularity supports robust ferromagnetism in the thermodynamic limit. This proves that DOS structure, not just degeneracy, is the controlling factor.
main_problem: To determine if band-minimum degeneracy alone is sufficient to stabilize low-density ferromagnetism in itinerant quantum many-body systems.
main_result: The stability of low-density ferromagnetism is controlled not by the mere degeneracy of band minima, but by the singular behavior (the strength) of the density of states at the band bottom.
method: Theoretical analysis using the T-matrix approximation to calculate ground state energies and compare finite-size versus thermodynamic limit results for different lattice models.
model_or_system: The study analyzes two geometries of the Fermi–Hubbard model realized in ultracold atoms within an optical lattice: one with one-diagonal hopping and another with two-diagonal hopping on a square lattice.
key_observables: Ferromagnetic phase stability, system size dependence (finite vs. thermodynamic limit), and the functional form of the density of states singularity at the band bottom.
important_parameters: Electron filling ($n$), interaction strength ($U/t$), hopping parameters ($t'/t$), and lattice dimensionality/hopping structure.
main_assumptions: The T-matrix approximation is assumed to be highly accurate in the dilute electron density limit, where correlations are dominated by two-body collisions.
figures_summary: Figures compare phase diagrams across different cluster sizes and interaction strengths for both hopping models, showing that ferromagnetism persists only in the thermodynamic limit for the two-diagonal model due to its stronger DOS singularity.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical context (ultracold atoms/Müller–Hartmann mechanism), compares two lattice models exhibiting band degeneracy, and systematically uses finite-size scaling and DOS analysis to prove that the strength of the DOS singularity dictates magnetic stability.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous theoretical counterexample showing that simple geometric symmetries or degeneracies are insufficient predictors for complex many-body phenomena like ferromagnetism, emphasizing the role of spectral structure (DOS) in quantum matter.
